cells.tense: You hold several true things about a person at once and you're in the room with them while you do it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you see clearly about someone near you and say it as a plain fact — one sentence, no cushioning — and notice what it's like when your read is out in the room instead of held.
cells.core:
You can carry more than one true thing about a person and stay close to them at the same time. What you notice doesn't turn into a case you're building; it stays something you know, and people feel the difference. When someone tells you what's going on with them, your read usually arrives fast and lands right, and you don't need them to agree before you can be kind. People bring you the harder version of the story.

What you see is worth more when it's shared. One clear thing about someone close to you is still sitting in your head. Say it to them this week — one sentence, no waiting for the right moment. It'll give them something solid to stand on, and it'll show you that your read can leave your head and survive being spoken.

cells.tense: You're reading several steps ahead of every conversation and living in the versions that haven't happened yet.
cells.ask: Take one thing you see about someone in your life — not a plan, not a warning — and say it to them once, then ask what they think: the sentence stays a sentence, and their answer has somewhere to land.
cells.core:
Knowing a lot about people is a real gift, and when it works, you can sit with someone and see them clearly without needing to fix or forecast anything. That's the version where your read stays in the present with them.

Lately the read runs ahead of the room. You've worked out how the conversation will go, what they'll say, where it ends up, and you're arranging yourself around a future that hasn't arrived. The person in front of you is getting your forecast instead of your attention. What you might be preserving is the small gap where you don't yet know, and that gap is where the conversation actually happens. Say one true thing you see and then stop — no follow-up, no preparing for their reaction — because a read spoken and answered is worth more than five that stayed in your head.

cells.tense: You saw what was true and it didn't go anywhere, so what you see now stays where it is.
cells.ask: Say one thought about someone close to you while it's still rough — in the room, unedited — and let their response land whatever it is, so what you see gets somewhere to go.
cells.core:
People can be met exactly as they are, and what you notice about them can shape how you treat them without being announced. In a good week this looks like a conversation where something true about the person surfaces and quietly changes how you hold them.

Right now what you see doesn't reach the room. You notice clear things about the people around you and mention none of it, and it stays in your own head. Two things move it back: letting someone else's view sit next to yours without having to settle which one wins, and choosing which direction you're actually trying to go with this person. Say one thought out loud while it's still rough. Let whatever comes back come back. The point is to get it out of the loop inside you and into the room where it can be tested.

cells.tense: You know what's right between you and the people around you, and the calls are running without you noticing they're yours.
cells.ask: Name one call you made recently about what was fair between you and someone — just say out loud or on paper that you made it — because a call you've said is yours is easier to trust the next time it points where your read doesn't expect.
cells.core:
When you're close to people, you know what's fair between you without having to work it out. It's a felt sense, not a calculation — you can tell when something is owed or when something's been paid, and you handle it gently. That's the version where things flow.

Right now it runs without you at the wheel. Small calls get made all day about what to say, what to let pass, what someone is owed, and they get described as if they made themselves. The fairness is real and the maker isn't. Naming one call as yours puts it back in your hand, and it's the one you'd want the next time someone asks whether something is fair.
cells.sheetLine: You're making the calls about what's fair — you're just not saying they're yours.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim risk here is describing what the person does with their knowing in company — whether they argue, explain, or hold the many truths to themselves — since the record only establishes the capacity, not the biography. A reader could reasonably say the arguing is just their way of caring, or that holding back is respect rather than a closed door; both are answerable, because the ask is one sentence said to one person about what they themselves see, not about how they should feel. The ask survives being wrong: if the many truths stay privately sorted, saying one of them aloud still shows the person something about what they hold. The sentence that serves the writer most is the Tense-2 close on becoming a verdict no one agreed to — it risks assigning an audience's experience the person never reported; it stays only because the ask brings it back to what the person says, not what anyone hears.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is in cell 2 and cell 4: I say what the person does with their knowing — forecasting conversations, glossing their own fair calls — and the record only establishes the capacity, not the behavior. A reader could reasonably say the forecasting is just being thorough, or that the fair calls are theirs and obviously so; both stand, because the ask asks them to do one thing, not to accept a description of themselves. The ask survives being wrong: saying one sentence to one person teaches something about the capacity even if the forecast picture doesn't fit, and naming one fair call as their own costs nothing if they already know it was. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader was cell 3's line about silence keeping something closed — it flavors the status with a motive; it's out, replaced by location only.
